title: The 8 Secrets of the 8-Step Espresso Routine
summary: Eight simple steps, done the same way every time. Here's the espresso routine we teach at our clinics – and the secret behind each step.
body: At our espresso clinics, we teach a simple eight-step routine. It isn't the only way to make espresso, but it's consistent, easy to remember and works on almost any machine. Here are the steps, and the secret behind each one. 1. Purge the group head. Run a little water through before you start. Secret: it stabilises temperature and rinses away old coffee. 2. Dry the basket. Wipe the portafilter clean and dry. Secret: water in the basket leads to uneven extraction. 3. Weigh your dose. Use a scale every time. Secret: half a gram can change the taste noticeably. 4. Distribute the grounds. Tap or use a tool to level the bed. Secret: even distribution prevents channelling. 5. Tamp level. Press firmly and evenly. Secret: a level tamp matters far more than how hard you press. 6. Lock in and start immediately. Don't let the portafilter sit in the hot group. Secret: waiting can scorch the top of the puck. 7. Watch and time the shot. Note the time and the yield. Secret: consistency comes from measuring, not guessing. 8. Taste and adjust. Sour? Grind finer. Bitter? Grind coarser. Secret: change only one thing at a time. That's it. Eight steps, done the same way, every time. The real secret is not any single step, but the routine itself. When the process is consistent, you can finally taste what your adjustments are doing. Practise it daily for two weeks and it will feel natural. Your espresso, and your confidence, will thank you.

title: Change: The Biggest Step Is Step Zero!
summary: Before the first step of any change, there's a step most people skip: deciding why you want it. Our series on change continues.
body: In this series, we've talked about the stages of change and how to break big goals into small steps. But there's one step that comes before all the others, and it's the one most people skip. We call it step zero. Step zero is deciding why. Why do you want to change your coffee habit? Not why you think you should, or why someone else wants you to. Why do you want it? This might sound obvious, but it makes an enormous difference. People who start a change without a clear reason often give up when it gets hard. People who know their why are much more likely to keep going. At our clinics, we ask new participants this question. The answers vary widely. "I want my morning coffee to be something I look forward to." "I want to understand what I'm tasting." "I want to stop spending so much money in cafés." "My partner loves coffee and I want to share that with them." Each of these is a good reason. And each one points to a different path. Someone who wants to save money needs a simple, reliable home setup. Someone who wants to understand tasting needs cupping sessions and side-by-side comparisons. Someone who wants to share a passion with a partner needs a ritual for two. Without step zero, people often choose the wrong path. They buy an expensive espresso machine when what they really wanted was a calm ten minutes in the morning. Then they feel frustrated and give up. So before you take your first step, sit down with a cup of whatever coffee you have now. Ask yourself: what do I really want from this? Write the answer down. Keep it somewhere you'll see it. It's a small step. In many ways, it's the biggest one.

title: Three Days at the Coffee House Retreat
summary: Three days in a farmhouse, twenty-four participants and more coffee than we care to admit. Participants share their thoughts from our autumn retreat.
body: In September, we held our first three-day Coffee House Retreat at a converted farmhouse in the countryside. Twenty-four participants, four instructors and a kitchen transformed into a brewing lab. We asked participants to share a few thoughts afterwards. "I came for the espresso lessons, but what I'll remember is the morning walks with coffee in our hands, watching the mist lift off the fields. I didn't know I needed that kind of quiet." – Esther "On the first day, I was too shy to say what I tasted. By the third day, I was arguing passionately that a Colombian tasted like rhubarb. Everyone was so welcoming that I forgot to be nervous." – Dennis "The roasting workshop changed how I see coffee completely. Watching the beans change colour, smelling every stage, I finally understood why freshness matters so much." – Judith "I've been brewing at home for years and thought I knew a lot. This retreat showed me how much more there is to learn, and that learning with others is much more fun than learning alone." – Frank "The evenings were my favourite. Sitting around the long table, sharing food, telling stories, drinking decaf so we could sleep. It felt like a family." – Kate As organisers, we were moved by how quickly the group became close. People arrived as strangers on Friday afternoon. By Sunday, they were exchanging phone numbers, planning visits to each other's favourite cafés and promising to meet at the next Cupping Day. We'll run the retreat again next year, with a few improvements: more blankets for the cold mornings, and a bigger milk fridge. If you'd like to join, keep an eye on our newsletter. Thank you to everyone who made these three days so special.

title: Movement Is Good for Coffee! – Why Agitation Matters
summary: Stirring, swirling, pouring from a height – agitation is one of the most underrated variables in brewing. Here's what moving the coffee bed actually does.
body: When home brewers try to improve their coffee, they usually think about three things: grind size, ratio and water temperature. All important. But there's a fourth variable that's often overlooked, even though it has a huge effect on the cup: agitation. Agitation simply means movement. Every time you pour water, stir the slurry or swirl the brewer, you move the coffee grounds around. And movement changes extraction. Here's why. When hot water touches coffee grounds, it starts dissolving flavour compounds from them. Right around each particle, the water quickly becomes saturated, full of dissolved coffee, and extraction slows down. Moving the water and grounds replaces that saturated layer with fresh water, so extraction speeds up again. More agitation means faster, more complete extraction. Less agitation means slower, gentler extraction. That's why two people using exactly the same recipe can get completely different results. One pours gently from close to the coffee bed; the other pours from high up in a strong stream. The second person's coffee will usually be more extracted, sometimes sweeter, sometimes more bitter. So how can you use this? If your coffee tastes sour or thin, try adding a little more agitation: a gentle stir after the bloom, a swirl at the end of the brew or pouring from slightly higher. If it tastes bitter or harsh, try the opposite: pour more gently and skip the stir. Agitation also helps with consistency. A gentle swirl at the end of a pour-over flattens the coffee bed, so water drains evenly instead of channelling through one side. Like everything in coffee, the key is to change one thing at a time and taste the difference. Movement is good for coffee, but the right amount of movement is what makes it great.

title: Our Free Brew Clinic Is Opening!
summary: Struggling with sour coffee, bitter espresso or a grinder you don't understand? Starting next month, Bloom & Burr offers free weekly brew clinics for everyone.
body: We're thrilled to announce something we've been dreaming about for a long time. Starting next month, Bloom & Burr will host a free weekly Brew Clinic, open to everyone, members or not. Why are we doing this? Because over the years, we've received hundreds of messages from people who are frustrated with their coffee at home. They've bought good beans and decent equipment, but something isn't working. Their coffee is sour, or bitter, or just boring. Many of them have tried to fix it alone for months. Often, the solution is simple: a grind adjustment, a different ratio, a change in pouring technique. But it's hard to see from the inside. A second pair of eyes, and a second palate, can make all the difference. Here's how the clinic works. Every Thursday evening, from six to eight, our experienced brew hosts will be at the café. Bring your own beans and, if possible, your own grinder and brewer. We'll watch you brew, taste the result together and help you find what needs to change. No question is too basic. No equipment is too cheap or too fancy. Whether you use a French press from the supermarket or a high-end espresso machine, you're welcome. The clinic is free because we believe good coffee shouldn't be a privilege. It's our way of giving back: sales from our beans, café and courses pay for it, and our brew hosts run it because they remember how it felt to be a frustrated beginner. If you'd like to join the clinic team one day, tell us. Several of our brew hosts started out as clinic regulars. You don't need to be a professional, just patient, friendly and curious. We can't wait to meet you. Bring your coffee, bring your questions and bring a friend. Let's make better coffee, together.

title: Following Our Intuition – Notes From the Blind Tasting Workshop
summary: No labels, no prices, no tasting notes. Just six cups and our own senses. Participants share what they discovered at our first blind tasting workshop.
body: In October we ran our first Blind Tasting Workshop. The idea was simple: six coffees, numbered cups, no information. Participants didn't know the origin, the roast level, the price or the roaster. They had only their senses and their intuition. We asked participants to share their impressions afterwards. Here are a few of their reflections. "I was sure I'd prefer the expensive coffee. I ended up loving cup number four, which turned out to be the cheapest one on the table. It was such a relief to realise I don't need to spend a fortune to enjoy great coffee." – Pippa "Without the labels, I stopped trying to taste what I was supposed to taste. I just tasted. It felt very freeing." – Adam "I usually say I don't like dark roasts. Then I picked a dark roast as my favourite. I'm still processing this." – Laura "The best part was hearing everyone's descriptions. One person said cup two tasted like a library. Another said it was like cherry pie. Both were somehow right." – Sophie "I came alone and was nervous. By the end, I was laughing with five people I'd never met. We exchanged numbers so we can taste together again." – Martin What struck us most as hosts was how much people trusted themselves by the end. At the start, many asked, "Is this right? Am I tasting it correctly?" By the last round, nobody asked that anymore. They simply said what they tasted. Labels and tasting notes are useful. But they can also become a cage, telling us what to expect before we've even sipped. Blind tasting removes that cage for a while and gives us back our own intuition. We'll be running another workshop in the spring. Bring your curiosity, and leave your expectations at the door.

title: Huff and Puff – Bean and the Art of Waiting for the Bloom
summary: Forty-five seconds. That's how long the bloom takes. Apparently, it's also exactly how long I can't stand still – until Bean showed me how.
body: I have a confession. I'm terrible at waiting for the bloom. For those who don't brew pour-over: the bloom is the first small pour of water onto fresh grounds. The coffee puffs up and releases gas, and you're supposed to wait about forty-five seconds before continuing. Forty-five seconds. It's nothing. And yet I always find myself fidgeting, checking my phone, tapping my foot, cutting it short. Yesterday Bean caught me at it again. "Thirty-one seconds," he said from my shoulder, peering at the timer. "New record for impatience." "It's fine," I muttered. "Nobody can taste fourteen seconds." "You can," he said. "You told me so yourself last week, in a very long speech about carbon dioxide." I sighed. He was right, of course. "Let's try something," Bean said. "Next time, don't look at the timer. Watch the coffee. Breathe in slowly while it rises. Breathe out while it settles. Do it three times. Then pour." It sounded silly. I tried it anyway. I poured the bloom and watched the coffee bed swell up like a tiny loaf of bread. I breathed in slowly. Small bubbles appeared on the surface. I breathed out. The crust cracked and darkened. Three breaths later I looked at the timer: forty-eight seconds. It hadn't felt like waiting at all. It had felt like watching something happen. "Our grandmothers knew this," Bean said, settling back into his cap. "They sang while the bread rose. They hummed while the soup simmered. Waiting is only boring when you're not paying attention." The coffee was noticeably sweeter. Or maybe I was just calmer when I drank it. Either way, I'll take it. So next time you're standing over a dripper, try the three-breath bloom. Huff and puff, slowly. The coffee doesn't need you to hurry, and neither does the day.

title: Christmas Cupping Day at the Old Mill
summary: Candles, spiced coffee, a crackling stove and sixty members in a converted mill. A short report from our favourite event of the winter.
body: Every December we hold one Cupping Day that's a little different from the others. Less about scores and tasting notes, more about warmth, light and being together before the busy holidays begin. This year we gathered at the old mill on the river, now a community centre with stone walls and a wonderful cast-iron stove. Sixty members came, along with a few curious neighbours who followed the smell of coffee down the lane. Our team had decorated the long tables with pine branches and candles, and there was a pot of spiced coffee with orange peel and cinnamon warming on the stove from the moment the doors opened. The cupping itself featured five coffees chosen for the season: a chocolatey Guatemalan, a sweet Peruvian with notes of dried fig, a festive natural Ethiopian that one participant described as "Christmas cake in a cup," a decaf from Colombia that surprised everyone with its sweetness, and a small lot from a Rwandan cooperative we've worked with for three years. Between the rounds, people swapped stories about holiday coffee traditions. Someone's family always makes egg coffee on Christmas morning. Another member brews a pot of cardamom coffee for the whole neighbourhood every year. A young couple shared that they met at our Christmas cupping two years ago and were celebrating their engagement. In the afternoon, children decorated paper coffee bags as gifts, while the adults learned to make a simple spiced syrup to take home. As the light faded outside, we turned off the main lamps and finished with a candlelit tasting of the Rwandan coffee, poured from a big pot into everyone's cups at the same time. For a few minutes, the only sounds were the stove and quiet sips. Thank you to everyone who came, to the team who stayed late to wash a mountain of cups, and to the guest roasters who brought their coffees. Wishing all of you a warm and peaceful season.

title: Only Winners Get to Cry – My First Latte Art Throwdown
summary: Guest author Rose Dalton signed up for a latte art throwdown on a dare. She didn't expect to cry – or to win.
body: I want to start by saying that I signed up as a joke. A friend from our Bloom & Burr clinic dared me, and I've never been good at refusing a dare. The throwdown was three weeks away. I could pour a wobbly heart on a good day. So I practised. Every evening after work I steamed milk and poured into cups of water mixed with cocoa powder, because I couldn't afford to waste that much coffee. My kitchen smelled like chocolate milk for three weeks. My partner started calling me "the tulip lady." On the night of the throwdown, there were sixteen of us. Real baristas, people from cafés I admired. I wanted to go home before it started. The Bloom & Burr team noticed and kept bringing me water and telling silly jokes until my hands stopped shaking. In the first round, I poured a three-layer tulip. It wasn't perfect, but it was the best one I had ever made. The judges picked mine. In the second round, I won again, barely. By the semi-final, I was in such disbelief that I forgot to breathe and poured a shape the host kindly described as "modern art." I lost that round. And then I cried, right there next to the espresso machine. The winner of the whole evening, a barista with ten years of experience, came over and put a hand on my shoulder. "You know what they say," he said. "Only winners get to cry. You just beat twelve professionals with a home setup and cocoa water. That's winning." I'll never forget that. We often think winning means coming first. But sometimes winning means showing up, being terrified and doing it anyway. Sometimes it means discovering that a whole room of strangers is cheering for you. I've entered three more throwdowns since then. I haven't won one yet. But I keep pouring tulips, and I keep crying a little at the end of every evening. Only winners get to cry, after all.

title: No Way But Forward
summary: When her café closed overnight, our guest author Nora Hall had a choice: give up coffee or reinvent it. She chose a bicycle.
body: Three years ago, I was the head barista at a busy café near the harbour. I loved that job: the regulars, the early light through the windows, the rhythm of a Saturday rush. Then one Monday morning the owner called us in and said the café was closing. Not in a month. That week. I remember walking home along the water feeling completely empty. Coffee had been my life for eight years. Now I had a box of aprons, a tamper I'd bought with my first paycheck and no idea what to do next. For a few weeks I applied for other café jobs. Nothing felt right. Then my brother, who repairs bicycles, showed me an old cargo bike someone had left at his shop. "You could put a coffee machine on that," he joked. I didn't laugh. I couldn't stop thinking about it. It took four months, a small loan and a lot of help from friends to build the cart. A lever espresso machine that doesn't need electricity, a hand grinder, a water tank and a little wooden sign that says "Forward Coffee." The name was my brother's idea. "There's no way but forward," he said. "So call it that." My first morning, I parked by the ferry terminal and sold fourteen coffees. My hands were shaking for most of them. By the end of the first summer, I had regulars again. Some of them were the same people from the old café, who had tracked me down. I found Bloom & Burr through a member who stopped by for a cortado. The community gave me advice on permits, roasters and how to keep a lever machine happy in cold weather. More importantly, it gave me people who understood why I'd want to brew espresso on a bicycle in November. I won't pretend the closure didn't hurt. It did. But looking back, it pushed me into something I would never have dared to try otherwise. If you're standing at the end of something right now, I can only tell you what helped me: take one small step. Then another. There really is no way but forward.

title: Eliza's Path: The Gift Behind a Failed Café
summary: Eliza poured her savings and her heart into a small café. Eighteen months later she had to close it. What she found on the other side surprised her.
body: Eliza opened her café on a rainy Tuesday in March. She had painted the walls herself, chosen every cup and spent two years saving for the espresso machine. On the first day, eleven customers came. She remembers every one of them. Eighteen months later, she turned the sign to "Closed" for the last time. Rents in the neighbourhood had doubled, a chain café had opened across the street and the winter had been brutally slow. "I cried for a week," she told me. "I felt like I had failed at the only thing I'd ever really wanted." For a while she couldn't even look at coffee. She took an office job, stopped going to cafés and put her grinder in a cupboard. Then, one Saturday, a former regular sent her a message. "We miss your coffee. Would you consider making it for our wedding?" Eliza said yes, mainly because she couldn't think of a polite way to say no. She set up a small bar in the corner of a garden, with her old grinder and a borrowed machine. She served two hundred guests in four hours. At the end of the night, three people asked for her number. Today, Eliza runs a mobile coffee service for weddings, festivals and company events. She works fewer hours than she did at the café, earns more and, as she puts it, "I finally get to talk to people instead of worrying about the rent." When I asked her whether she regrets the café, she thought for a long time. "No," she said finally. "It hurt. But everything I know about people, about service, about making coffee under pressure, I learned there. The café didn't fail me. It trained me." Not every ending is a defeat. Sometimes the thing that breaks our heart is also the thing that prepares us for what comes next. Eliza's path wasn't the one she planned. It turned out to be the one that fit.

title: Doing Nothing – An Afternoon in a Botanical Garden Café
summary: Our guest author, food scientist Dr. Iris Carter, spent an afternoon doing absolutely nothing in a small garden café. Here's what she tasted.
body: As a food scientist, I spend my working days measuring things. Extraction yields, particle sizes, acidity levels. I love it. But a few weeks ago, after a particularly long week in the lab, I promised myself an afternoon with no measurements at all. I went to a small café hidden in the corner of the city's botanical garden. It's a glass pavilion surrounded by ferns and old palm trees, with six tables, one espresso machine and a barista who seems to be in no hurry whatsoever. I ordered a filter coffee, a washed coffee from Burundi, and sat by the window. Then I did nothing. It was surprisingly difficult. My hands kept reaching for my phone. My mind kept analysing the coffee: medium body, clear citric acidity, a black tea finish, probably brewed a little coarse. I had to remind myself, gently, that today I was not a scientist. I was just a person drinking coffee in a garden. Slowly, something changed. I started noticing the sound of water dripping from the leaves after the gardener's hose. The smell of damp soil mixing with the coffee's aroma. A blackbird hopping between the tables, looking for crumbs. The way the light moved across the cup as clouds passed over the glass roof. The coffee tasted different, too. Not better in any measurable way, but more complete. Without trying to analyse it, I simply enjoyed it, and I remembered why I fell in love with coffee in the first place, long before I knew what a refractometer was. We are often told to make every minute productive. But some of the most important things, rest, ideas, connection, only appear when we stop chasing them. I stayed for two hours and drank two cups. I didn't take a single note. It was one of the best afternoons I've had all year.

title: Five Years of Bloom & Burr
summary: Five years ago, a handful of home brewers met in a borrowed kitchen. Today we are a community of thousands. A small look back – and a big thank you.
body: Five years ago, seven of us met in a borrowed community kitchen with two grinders, a box of mismatched cups and a bag of coffee from a roaster who had agreed, slightly confused, to sponsor our first cupping. We didn't have a name yet. We didn't have a plan. For two years we ran a weekend pop-up, carrying our grinders from one borrowed kitchen to the next, until we signed the lease on a small roastery with a café at the front. We had a shared feeling that good coffee was too often kept behind a wall of jargon and price tags, and that it didn't have to be. Today Bloom & Burr is a roastery, a café and a brewing school, with a community of more than three thousand members. We've run over two hundred brew clinics, sixty Cupping Days, five Brew Camps and countless late-night forum discussions about grind size. Our knowledge base is read by people in more than forty countries. But numbers are only half the story. The other half is the people. There's the retired teacher who now roasts on her balcony and brings us samples every month. The teenager who learned to pour latte art at our clinic and won his first local throwdown last spring. The café owner who found her head barista at one of our events. The couple who met over a blind tasting and argued, happily, about whether a coffee tasted like plums or cherries. None of this would exist without our team of baristas, roasters and brew hosts, who carry kettles, wash hundreds of cups and welcome nervous beginners with a smile. Without the roasters and farmers who share their coffees and stories. And without every member who has ever asked a question, shared a recipe or brought a friend. For our anniversary we want to say a simple thank you. You have turned a borrowed kitchen into a real home for coffee lovers. Next month we'll celebrate with a free Cupping Day, open to everyone, members or not. There will be coffees from five producers we've worked with since the beginning, and a cake that may or may not contain espresso. Here's to the next five years. Bring your cup.
